stem: A 24-year-old woman has had painful mouth sores that return every few months for several years. Each sore heals in about a week, and citrus or spicy food makes the pain worse. She has no fever, rash, genital ulcers, eye symptoms, joint pain, or bowel symptoms. Exam shows a shallow 5-mm ulcer with a white-gray base and a red rim on the inner lip.
oneliner: 24F + painful mouth ulcers every few months, each heals in ~1 wk + shallow ulcer, white base, red rim + no fever/rash/genital/eye/joint/GI symptoms → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Fever, sore throat, and posterior pharyngeal vesicles** in a child; this is a recurrent, afebrile adult
whyNot.B: Needs **genital ulcers or eye disease** with the oral ulcers; none here
whyNot.D: Grouped **vesicles on the lip border or skin**, not a shallow ulcer on inner mucosa
whyNot.E: Has a **diffuse rash (palms, soles)** or mucous patches; she has no rash and the ulcers are painful and recurrent

answer: Aphthous stomatitis (recurrent aphthous ulcers, canker sores)
why: **Recurrent shallow painful ulcers with a white base and red halo** in an otherwise healthy person with **no systemic features** = aphthous stomatitis.

stem: A 48-year-old man has swelling and pain in front of the right ear that start when he eats and settle afterward; he has no fever, and a firm nodule is felt inside the cheek at the opening of the parotid duct.
oneliner: 48M + cheek swelling in front of ear with meals, settles after + no fever + firm nodule at duct opening inside cheek → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: Gives **fever, malaise, and usually bilateral swelling**; his swelling is unilateral, meal-related, afebrile
whyNot.C: Has **fever, erythema, and pus from the duct**; none stated here
whyNot.D: **Dry eyes and dry mouth with bilateral gland enlargement**, not meal-triggered pain with a palpable nodule
whyNot.E: A **painless slow-growing mass** unrelated to meals

why: **Meal-triggered swelling and pain** with a **palpable stone at the duct opening** and no fever = sialolithiasis.

stem: A 28-year-old man has had trouble swallowing for 8 months. Both solids and liquids stick, and he sometimes regurgitates undigested food. He has lost 6 kg and has no heartburn. A barium swallow shows a dilated esophagus that tapers smoothly to a narrow end at the gastroesophageal junction, like a bird's beak.
oneliner: 28M + dysphagia to solids AND liquids x 8 mo + regurgitates undigested food + 6 kg weight loss + no heartburn + bird-beak on barium → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Main symptom is **heartburn**; he has none and no beak-like narrowing
whyNot.B: Shows a **patulous, wide-open lower sphincter** with reflux and skin or Raynaud features, not a tight beak
whyNot.C: An **older patient with an irregular mass or shouldered stricture**, not a smooth taper at age 28
whyNot.D: Barium shows a **corkscrew esophagus** with episodic chest pain, not a dilated esophagus with a beak

why: **Dysphagia to solids and liquids** in a young adult with **dilated esophagus and bird-beak tapering** = achalasia (failed lower esophageal sphincter relaxation).

stem: A 41-year-old man who grew up in a rural area of Brazil has had difficulty swallowing and has lost 7 kg over a year. He regurgitates food at night. A barium swallow shows a markedly dilated esophagus that narrows to a smooth, beak-like segment at the lower sphincter.
oneliner: 41M + grew up rural Brazil + dysphagia + 7 kg weight loss + nocturnal regurgitation + dilated esophagus with smooth beak on barium → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: A tumor gives an **irregular, shouldered stricture**, not a smooth beak above a massively dilated esophagus
whyNot.C: Barium shows a **corkscrew pattern** with chest pain; esophagus is not dilated
whyNot.D: Features **skin tightening and a wide-open lower sphincter**; here the sphincter is narrowed
whyNot.E: Long history of **heartburn** and a short distal stricture; there is no heartburn and the esophagus is dilated

answer: Achalasia, secondary to Chagas disease (Trypanosoma cruzi)
why: **Rural Brazil exposure** plus a **dilated esophagus with a smooth beak** = achalasia from Chagas destruction of myenteric neurons.

stem: A 71-year-old man has had difficulty swallowing for a year. Hours after meals he regurgitates undigested food, his breath smells foul, and he hears gurgling in his neck when he swallows. A barium swallow is shown.
oneliner: 71M + dysphagia + regurgitates undigested food hours later + halitosis + neck gurgling + [barium swallow] → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Barium shows a **dilated body tapering to a beak at the lower sphincter**; here the outpouching is high in the neck
whyNot.B: Would show an **irregular narrowing or mass**, not a smooth contrast-filled pouch
whyNot.C: A **thin shelf-like ridge** in the upper esophagus, not a pouch that holds food
whyNot.E: **Corkscrew contractions** with chest pain, no pouch

why: **Regurgitation of old undigested food, halitosis, and neck gurgling** with a **posterior hypopharyngeal pouch** = Zenker diverticulum.

stem: A 45-year-old man has had burning behind the breastbone for 10 years. It is worse after large meals and when he lies down, and he sometimes tastes acid in his throat. He has no trouble swallowing and has not lost weight. Endoscopy shows redness and a few shallow erosions limited to the distal esophagus.
oneliner: 45M + burning retrosternal pain x 10 y, worse after big meals and lying down + sour taste + no dysphagia/weight loss + distal erosions on endoscopy → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Endoscopy shows **salmon-colored columnar tongues** of mucosa; here only red erosions
whyNot.C: Presents with **dysphagia or food impaction, atopy, and rings or furrows**; he has none
whyNot.D: Main symptom is **dysphagia to solids and liquids with regurgitation**; this is heartburn without dysphagia
whyNot.E: **White plaques** in an immunocompromised patient with odynophagia, not erosions with heartburn

why: **Chronic meal- and position-related heartburn with acid regurgitation** and **distal erosions**, without alarm features = GERD.

stem: A 38-year-old man has burning behind the breastbone after large fatty meals and after evenings of heavy drinking. It is worse when he lies flat and antacids relieve it briefly. He has no trouble swallowing, no weight loss, and no vomiting of blood. Exam and ECG are normal.
oneliner: 38M + retrosternal burning after fatty meals/binge drinking, worse supine, antacids help briefly + no dysphagia/weight loss/hematemesis + normal ECG → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Epigastric** pain that changes with food timing, not postural retrosternal burning
whyNot.B: **Chest pain with swallowing** or cold liquids, not triggered by lying flat
whyNot.C: **Epigastric discomfort with nausea or vomiting**, no positional heartburn
whyNot.D: **Early satiety, bloating, and vomiting of old food**, none present

why: **Retrosternal burning after fatty meals and alcohol, worse supine**, relieved by antacids = GERD (lower esophageal sphincter relaxation).

stem: A 29-year-old woman at 24 weeks' gestation has burning in the chest after meals that is worse when she lies down. It started in the first trimester. Blood pressure is 112/70 mm Hg, urine protein is negative, and her abdomen is soft and non-tender.
oneliner: 29F + 24 wk pregnant + postprandial chest burning, worse lying down + BP 112/70, no proteinuria, soft non-tender abdomen → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Epigastric pain with food relation and possible melena**; this is retrosternal and positional
whyNot.B: Needs **high blood pressure and proteinuria**; both normal here
whyNot.D: **Right upper quadrant pain, fever, and tenderness**; abdomen is non-tender
whyNot.E: **Dysphagia and regurgitation**, not postprandial burning

why: **Positional postprandial heartburn in pregnancy** with normal vitals and labs = GERD (progesterone lowers lower esophageal sphincter tone).

stem: A 3-month-old boy spits up small amounts of milk after most feeds but is happy, feeds eagerly, and is growing along the 50th percentile; the spit-up is never green, forceful, or bloody.
oneliner: 3-mo M + small spit-ups after most feeds + happy, eager feeder, normal growth + never green/forceful/bloody → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **Projectile vomiting** with hunger and poor weight gain at 2-6 weeks; his spit-up is small and he is thriving
whyNot.C: **Bilious vomiting**; none here
whyNot.D: Presents at the **first feeds with choking and cyanosis**, not months of small spit-ups
whyNot.E: **Blood in stool, eczema, or irritability** with feeds; none described

why: **Small, effortless spit-ups in a thriving, happy infant** with no red flags = physiologic gastroesophageal reflux.

stem: A 58-year-old man has had heartburn for 20 years. Endoscopy shows abnormal-looking mucosa just above the gastroesophageal junction, and a biopsy is taken. The biopsy is shown.
oneliner: 58M + 20 y heartburn + abnormal mucosa just above GEJ + [biopsy] → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: The lining is still **squamous with basal hyperplasia**; here it is replaced by glands
whyNot.B: Squamous epithelium with **>15 eosinophils per high-power field**, not columnar cells
whyNot.C: Shows **invasive irregular glands and malignant cells**; this lining is orderly without invasion
whyNot.E: **Keratin pearls and atypical squamous cells**, not mucin-containing goblet cells

why: **Long-standing reflux** and **goblet cell intestinal metaplasia in the distal esophagus** = Barrett esophagus.

image.prompt: H&E-stained section of esophageal mucosa where the normal stratified squamous lining is replaced by columnar glandular epithelium containing numerous pale blue-gray goblet cells with mucin vacuoles; no invasion or marked atypia.

stem: A 62-year-old man who smokes two packs a day has had nighttime heartburn for 15 years. Endoscopy shows erosions in the distal esophagus. A biopsy shows that the squamous lining is replaced by columnar epithelium with goblet cells; there is no invasion.
oneliner: 62M + 2 ppd smoker + nocturnal heartburn x 15 y + distal erosions + biopsy: columnar epithelium with goblet cells, no invasion → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Smoking is a risk factor, but biopsy shows **glandular goblet cells, not malignant squamous cells**
whyNot.B: Biopsy would show **dense eosinophils in squamous epithelium**, with dysphagia and atopy
whyNot.C: **White plaques and yeast with pseudohyphae** in an immunocompromised host
whyNot.E: **Dysphagia to solids and liquids** with a dilated esophagus; here the history is reflux and the biopsy shows metaplasia

answer: Barrett esophagus (intestinal metaplasia from chronic GERD)
why: **Chronic reflux** with **goblet cell (intestinal) metaplasia** replacing esophageal squamous epithelium and **no invasion** = Barrett esophagus.

stem: A 63-year-old man who smokes and drinks heavily has had trouble swallowing, first with solids and now with liquids, and has lost 10 kg in 3 months. He has no history of heartburn. Endoscopy shows an ulcerated mass with raised edges in the mid-esophagus.
oneliner: 63M + heavy smoker/drinker + progressive dysphagia (solids then liquids) + 10 kg weight loss + no heartburn hx + ulcerated mid-esophageal mass → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: Arises in the **distal esophagus from Barrett metaplasia** after long reflux; this mass is mid-esophageal with no heartburn
whyNot.C: A **young patient with a smooth beak** and no mass
whyNot.D: A **smooth, short distal narrowing** after years of heartburn, not an ulcerated mid-esophageal mass
whyNot.E: A **smooth submucosal mass with intact overlying mucosa** and no weight loss

why: **Smoking and alcohol**, **progressive dysphagia with weight loss**, and an **ulcerated mid-esophageal mass** without reflux history = esophageal squamous cell carcinoma.

oneliner: 66M + heavy smoker/drinker + progressive dysphagia, solids then liquids + [barium swallow] → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Seen in the **distal esophagus after years of reflux**; this lesion is mid-esophageal in a smoker/drinker

whyNot.D: A **smooth, short distal narrowing** after long-standing heartburn
whyNot.E: A **smooth filling defect with sharp edges**, not an irregular shouldered stricture

stem: A 4-year-old girl is found beside an open bottle of drain cleaner and now drools and cries when she swallows; no object is missing from the home.
oneliner: 4F + found by open drain-cleaner (lye) bottle + drooling + odynophagia → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Needs a **swallowed object** such as a coin; here the exposure is a chemical
whyNot.B: Occurs in **immunocompromised patients** with punched-out ulcers; she is healthy
whyNot.C: **Gradual dysphagia to solids** in iron deficiency, not acute pain after exposure
whyNot.D: **Slowly progressive dysphagia** over months, not sudden pain after a chemical exposure

why: **Alkali (drain cleaner) exposure** followed by **drooling and painful swallowing** = caustic esophageal injury (liquefactive necrosis, later stricture).

stem: A 70-year-old woman started a once-weekly tablet after a vertebral fracture. She took the first one at bedtime with a sip of water and then lay down. Two days later she developed sharp pain on swallowing; she has not vomited. Endoscopy shows several discrete shallow erosions in the esophagus; the stomach and duodenum look normal.
oneliner: 70F + new weekly pill after vertebral fracture, taken with little water, then lay down + 2 d later sharp pain on swallowing, no vomiting + discrete esophageal erosions, normal stomach/duodenum → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: The **stomach and duodenum are normal**; no ulcer is seen
whyNot.C: A **linear tear with hematemesis after repeated retching**; she has not vomited
whyNot.D: **Painless bleeding in cirrhosis or portal hypertension**, not odynophagia; endoscopy shows erosions, not varices
whyNot.E: Years of **heartburn**; this began 2 days after a new pill with pain on swallowing

why: A **new bisphosphonate taken with little water while lying down**, then **odynophagia and discrete esophageal erosions** = pill esophagitis.

stem: A 52-year-old man has had burning epigastric pain for 3 months that begins 2 to 3 hours after meals and eases when he eats. He has lost 3 kg and passed one dark stool. He takes no NSAIDs and has no diarrhea. Endoscopy shows a 1-cm punched-out ulcer in the duodenal bulb, and a rapid urease test on an antral biopsy is positive.
oneliner: 52M + epigastric burning 2-3 h after meals, relieved by food + 3 kg loss + no NSAIDs/diarrhea + punched-out duodenal bulb ulcer, urease positive → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Duodenal ulcer due to Helicobacter pylori (peptic ulcer disease)

whyNot.B: Gives **multiple or distal ulcers with diarrhea**; this is a single bulb ulcer without diarrhea
whyNot.C: He **takes no NSAIDs** and the ulcer is duodenal, urease positive
whyNot.D: Pain **worsens with eating** with early satiety; here a benign punched-out duodenal ulcer eases with food
whyNot.E: **Normal endoscopy**; he has a visible ulcer

answer: Peptic ulcer disease (H. pylori duodenal ulcer)
why: **Pain 2-3 hours after meals relieved by food**, a **duodenal bulb ulcer**, and **positive urease test** = H. pylori peptic ulcer.

stem: A 67-year-old woman with knee osteoarthritis has taken ibuprofen 800 mg three times daily for 6 months. She has burning epigastric pain that wakes her at night, and today she passed black, tarry stool. She has not vomited. Stool antigen testing for Helicobacter pylori is negative. Endoscopy shows a 1.5-cm ulcer with smooth margins on the lesser curvature of the stomach.
oneliner: 67F + ibuprofen 800 mg tid x 6 mo + night epigastric burning + melena + no vomiting + H. pylori negative + smooth-edged gastric ulcer → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Stool antigen is negative**; the cause here is chronic NSAID use
whyNot.B: **Multiple refractory ulcers with diarrhea**; this is a single ulcer without diarrhea
whyNot.C: Bleeding follows **forceful retching**; she has not vomited and has a gastric ulcer
whyNot.E: The ulcer has **smooth margins**, not an irregular mass with heaped-up edges

why: **Chronic ibuprofen use** (reduced prostaglandin protection), **melena**, and a **benign gastric ulcer** with negative H. pylori = NSAID peptic ulcer.

stem: A 58-year-old man has had months of epigastric burning that improves with food. An hour ago he developed sudden severe upper abdominal pain. He lies still and his abdomen is rigid with rebound tenderness. He has not vomited. An upright chest x-ray is shown.
oneliner: 58M + months of epigastric burning + sudden severe abdominal pain + rigid abdomen, rebound + no vomiting + [upright CXR] → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Pain **radiates to the back with vomiting**, and the x-ray would not show free air
whyNot.B: Shows **dilated loops with air-fluid levels** and vomiting, not free air
whyNot.D: Follows **forceful vomiting** and shows mediastinal air or pleural effusion; he has not vomited
whyNot.E: Pain **starts periumbilical and moves to the right lower quadrant**; no ulcer history and no free air

why: **Ulcer history**, **sudden severe pain with a rigid abdomen**, and **free air under the diaphragm** = perforated peptic ulcer.

stem: A 44-year-old man has burning epigastric pain 1 to 2 hours after meals that has not improved after 8 weeks of a proton pump inhibitor and a full course of Helicobacter pylori therapy. He has several loose stools a day and has passed black stool. Endoscopy shows ulcers in the duodenum and beyond the bulb, with thick gastric folds. CT shows a 2-cm mass in the pancreatic head. He has no rash and his glucose is normal.
oneliner: 44M + postprandial epigastric burning refractory to PPI and H. pylori therapy + diarrhea + melena + ulcers beyond duodenal bulb, thick gastric folds + pancreatic head mass + no rash, normal glucose → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Profuse watery diarrhea with hypokalemia and low acid**; he has ulcers and high acid output
whyNot.B: **Necrolytic migratory erythema and diabetes**; no rash and normal glucose
whyNot.C: **Painless jaundice and weight loss** without recurrent multiple ulcers
whyNot.D: **Episodic hypoglycemia** with Whipple triad; his glucose is normal

why: **Refractory multiple ulcers beyond the duodenal bulb**, **diarrhea**, thick gastric folds, and a **pancreatic neuroendocrine mass** = gastrinoma (Zollinger-Ellison syndrome).

stem: A 47-year-old woman has epigastric pain that eases after meals and has improved only partly on a proton pump inhibitor. One week after the PPI is stopped, fasting serum gastrin is 1,200 pg/mL (normal <100 pg/mL) and gastric pH is 1.4.
oneliner: 47F + epigastric pain eased by meals, partial PPI response + off PPI 1 wk: gastrin 1,200 pg/mL (nl <100), gastric pH 1.4 → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Gastrin is **normal or only mildly raised**, not more than 10-fold
whyNot.C: Gastrin is high but acid is **low (gastric pH high)**; her pH is 1.4
whyNot.D: PPIs raise gastrin by **suppressing acid (high gastric pH)**; she is off the PPI with pH 1.4 and gastrin >10 times normal
whyNot.E: **Normal gastrin** with no ulcer or hypersecretion

why: **Gastrin more than 10 times normal off the PPI with gastric pH <2** = autonomous gastrin secretion, Zollinger-Ellison syndrome.

stem: A 33-year-old woman under heavy work stress has had gnawing epigastric pain for a year, with only slight relief from an H2 blocker; her exam, blood tests, and endoscopy are normal, and she has no weight loss or low mood.
oneliner: 33F + high work stress + gnawing epigastric pain x 1 y, little H2 blocker effect + normal exam, labs, endoscopy + no weight loss or low mood → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Needs an **ulcer on endoscopy**; the study is normal
whyNot.B: Would show a **mass or thickened folds with weight loss**; neither is present
whyNot.D: Pain is **related to defecation with altered stool habit**; hers is epigastric
whyNot.E: Requires **low mood or loss of interest**; she reports none

why: **Chronic epigastric pain with a normal endoscopy and exam** in a stressed patient, no alarm features = functional dyspepsia.

stem: A 74-year-old woman with a known large hiatal hernia suddenly develops severe pain in the lower chest and upper abdomen. She retches repeatedly but cannot vomit. Blood pressure is 82/50 mm Hg, and a nasogastric tube cannot be passed. Chest x-ray shows an air-fluid level behind the heart and no free air.
oneliner: 74F + known large hiatal hernia + sudden lower chest/epigastric pain + retching, cannot vomit + hypotension + NG tube will not pass + retrocardiac air-fluid level, no free air → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: Gives **free air under the diaphragm** and a rigid abdomen; there is none here
whyNot.C: Pain **radiates to the back with vomiting**, and it would not block an NG tube
whyNot.D: **Right upper quadrant pain, fever, and Murphy sign**, not retching with a blocked tube
whyNot.E: Develops over **weeks to months with weight loss**, not sudden obstruction

why: **Sudden pain, retching without vomiting, and inability to pass an NG tube** (Borchardt triad) with a hiatal hernia = gastric volvulus.

stem: A newborn girl, born after a pregnancy with polyhydramnios, drools frothy saliva and chokes at her first feed; a feeding tube stops 10 cm from the lips, and x-ray shows gas in the stomach.
oneliner: Newborn girl + polyhydramnios + drooling, frothy saliva, choking at 1st feed + feeding tube stops at 10 cm + gas in stomach → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Causes **vomiting after feeds with a double-bubble** and the tube passes into the stomach
whyNot.B: Presents with **respiratory distress and a scaphoid abdomen**, with bowel in the chest
whyNot.C: The abdomen is **gasless**; here gas reaches the stomach
whyNot.D: Appears at **2-6 weeks with projectile vomiting**, not at the first feed

answer: Esophageal atresia with distal tracheoesophageal fistula
why: **Drooling, choking at first feed, a tube that will not pass, polyhydramnios, and gas in the stomach** = esophageal atresia with distal TEF.

stem: A 4-week-old firstborn boy has projectile nonbilious vomiting after every feed and is hungry again right afterward; waves of peristalsis are seen crossing his upper abdomen.
oneliner: 4-wk-old M + projectile nonbilious vomiting after every feed + hungry afterward + visible gastric peristaltic waves → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Presents in the **first days of life with a double-bubble**, not at 4 weeks
whyNot.C: **Choking and drooling at the first feed**, from birth
whyNot.D: **Colicky pain and currant-jelly stool** at 6-36 months
whyNot.E: **Delayed meconium and constipation with distension**, not projectile vomiting

why: **Projectile nonbilious vomiting at 2-6 weeks, hunger after vomiting, and visible peristalsis** = hypertrophic pyloric stenosis.

stem: A 5-week-old boy has had projectile nonbilious vomiting after every feed for 5 days and is eager to feed again right after vomiting. He is dehydrated. Labs show Na 134 mEq/L, K 3.0 mEq/L, Cl 88 mEq/L, HCO3 33 mEq/L, and arterial pH 7.50.

whyNot.B: Presents in the **first days of life with a double-bubble**, not at 5 weeks
whyNot.C: **Small, effortless spit-ups** with normal electrolytes in a thriving infant
whyNot.E: Brings **diarrhea and fever**, with acidosis from stool bicarbonate loss rather than alkalosis

why: **Projectile nonbilious vomiting at 5 weeks, hunger afterward, and hypochloremic hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis** = hypertrophic pyloric stenosis.

stem: A 2-week-old boy vomits green fluid after every feed and has lost weight; abdominal x-ray shows a double-bubble sign.
oneliner: 2-wk-old M + green vomiting after every feed + weight loss + double bubble on x-ray → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Vomit is **nonbilious and projectile**, with no double-bubble
whyNot.C: Causes **drooling and choking at the first feed**, not bilious vomiting
whyNot.D: Gives **effortless regurgitation or reflux**, not bilious obstruction
whyNot.E: Causes **painless rectal bleeding**, not vomiting with a double-bubble

why: **Bilious vomiting after every feed with a double-bubble** (obstruction below the ampulla) = annular pancreas, a ring of pancreas around the second part of the duodenum.

stem: An 8-year-old girl with normal development has had months of epigastric pain and green vomiting after meals; CT shows pancreatic tissue encircling the second part of the duodenum.
oneliner: 8F + normal development + months of epigastric pain + green vomiting after meals + CT: pancreatic tissue encircling 2nd part of duodenum → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Occurs at **2-6 weeks of age with nonbilious projectile vomiting**
whyNot.B: Shows up **at birth with drooling and choking**
whyNot.C: Presents with **jaundice, pale stools, and dark urine** in early infancy
whyNot.D: CT would show **no pancreatic tissue around the duodenum**

why: **Bilious vomiting and epigastric pain** with **pancreatic tissue encircling the second part of the duodenum** = annular pancreas.

stem: A 2-day-old full-term boy has sudden bilious vomiting and a distended, tender abdomen, and passes a dark red stool. Abdominal x-ray shows few gas-filled loops beyond the stomach and duodenum and no double-bubble sign.
oneliner: 2-day-old term M + sudden bilious vomiting + distended tender abdomen + dark red stool + paucity of distal gas, no double bubble → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Shows a **double-bubble** and is not usually accompanied by bloody stool
whyNot.B: Also gives a **double-bubble**, with a non-distended, soft abdomen
whyNot.D: **Nonbilious projectile vomiting** at weeks of age
whyNot.E: Affects **premature infants with pneumatosis intestinalis**; he is full-term and the film shows no intramural gas

why: **Bilious vomiting, a distended tender abdomen, and bloody stool** in a newborn = midgut volvulus from malrotation, a twist of the SMA pedicle.

stem: A 34-year-old woman has had 2 days of colicky abdominal pain with vomiting. She has never had abdominal surgery, and her heart and liver are on the normal sides. An upper GI series is shown.

whyNot.C: **Colicky pain, lethargy, and currant-jelly stool**; he is alert and pain-free
whyNot.E: An older adult with **left lower quadrant pain and fever**, not a toddler with painless bleeding

why: **Large painless maroon rectal bleeding in a toddler** with anemia and a benign abdomen = Meckel diverticulum (acid from ectopic gastric mucosa ulcerates the ileum).

stem: A 19-year-old man has fever and right lower quadrant pain. He had an appendectomy at age 12, and the pathology report confirmed the appendix was removed. Over the past two years he has had two episodes of dark red stool without pain. He has no chronic diarrhea or weight loss. A technetium-99m pertechnetate scan shows uptake in the right lower abdomen.
oneliner: 19M + fever + RLQ pain + appendectomy at 12 + 2 earlier painless dark red stools + no chronic diarrhea/weight loss + Tc-99m scan: RLQ uptake → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: The **appendix was already removed**
whyNot.B: **Chronic diarrhea, weight loss, and cramps**; he has neither
whyNot.C: **Colicky pain with a palpable mass** and a lead point, and no uptake on pertechnetate scan
whyNot.E: Brings **flushing and diarrhea** and does not take up pertechnetate

answer: Meckel diverticulum (inflamed, with ectopic gastric mucosa)
why: **Appendicitis-like pain after appendectomy**, **prior painless bleeding**, and **pertechnetate uptake** (gastric mucosa) = Meckel diverticulum.

stem: A 12-year-old boy has had recurrent periumbilical pain for several months. At surgery the appendix is normal. A 5-cm blind-ended pouch arises from the antimesenteric border of the ileum about 60 cm from the ileocecal valve, and its lining contains gastric-type mucosa.
oneliner: 12M + months of recurrent periumbilical pain + OR: normal appendix, 5-cm antimesenteric ileal pouch ~60 cm from ileocecal valve, gastric-type lining → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: The **appendix is normal**
whyNot.C: Shows **skip lesions, wall thickening, and strictures**, not a solitary pouch with a normal remaining bowel
whyNot.D: Projects **into the lumen**; this is an outpouching on the antimesenteric wall
whyNot.E: Needs a **telescoped segment with a mass**, which is not described

why: A **true antimesenteric ileal outpouching ~2 feet from the ileocecal valve** with **gastric mucosa** = Meckel diverticulum (persistent vitelline duct remnant).

stem: A 10-day-old boy has continuous drainage of green-yellow, stool-like fluid from the umbilicus after the cord has separated, and a contrast study shows a tract running from the umbilicus to the ileum.
oneliner: 10-day-old M + umbilical drainage of stool-like fluid + contrast tract from umbilicus to ileum → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Drains **clear, urine-like fluid** from a tract to the bladder
whyNot.B: **Viscera inside a membranous sac** at the base of the cord at birth
whyNot.D: A **moist pink nodule** with serous drainage and no tract to bowel
whyNot.E: **Bowel outside the abdomen without a sac**, lateral to an intact cord

answer: Patent vitelline duct (omphalomesenteric fistula), related to Meckel diverticulum
why: **Enteric drainage from the umbilicus** along a **tract to the ileum** = persistent vitelline (omphalomesenteric) duct.

stem: A 3-week-old term girl has progressive jaundice with pale stools and dark urine, and total bilirubin is 8.0 mg/dL with a direct fraction of 6.5 mg/dL.
oneliner: 3-wk-old term F + progressive jaundice + pale stools + dark urine + total bili 8.0, direct 6.5 mg/dL → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Unconjugated** hyperbilirubinemia with normal stool color and no bilirubin in urine
whyNot.B: Mild **unconjugated** jaundice that shows up later with stress or fasting
whyNot.C: **Unconjugated** bilirubin with anemia and a positive Coombs test
whyNot.D: **Unconjugated**, appears day 2-3 and resolves by about 2 weeks, with normal stool color

why: **Persistent jaundice beyond 2 weeks with pale stools, dark urine, and direct hyperbilirubinemia** = biliary atresia.

stem: A 5-week-old girl has been jaundiced since the second week of life and passes pale stools. Direct bilirubin is elevated and alpha-1 antitrypsin phenotype is normal. Ultrasound shows a small gallbladder and no cyst. A hepatobiliary scan shows liver uptake but no tracer in the bowel at 24 hours. Liver biopsy shows bile duct proliferation, portal fibrosis, and bile plugs.
oneliner: 5-wk-old F + jaundice since wk 2 + pale stools + direct hyperbili + normal alpha-1 antitrypsin + HIDA: no bowel excretion + biopsy: ductular proliferation, portal fibrosis → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Her **phenotype is normal**
whyNot.C: Biopsy shows **giant cells and hepatocellular inflammation**, and the scan shows bowel excretion
whyNot.D: Ultrasound shows a **cystic dilation of the bile duct**; none here
whyNot.E: Biopsy shows **paucity of bile ducts**, with typical facies and vertebral anomalies; here ducts are proliferating

why: **Pale stools, direct hyperbilirubinemia, no bowel excretion on the scan, and ductular proliferation with portal fibrosis** = biliary atresia.

stem: A 1-day-old full-term boy has not passed meconium, and an abdominal x-ray shows dilated small-bowel loops with a ground-glass appearance in the right lower quadrant; his older brother has cystic fibrosis.
oneliner: 1-day-old term M + no meconium passed + dilated small bowel, ground-glass RLQ on x-ray + brother with CF → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: Shows a **narrow aganglionic rectosigmoid with proximally dilated colon**, not a ground-glass small bowel
whyNot.C: Appears at **2-6 weeks with projectile vomiting**
whyNot.D: Causes **painless rectal bleeding** in toddlers
whyNot.E: **Fat malabsorption with acanthocytes** appearing after feeds begin, not obstruction on day 1

why: **No meconium, dilated small bowel with ground-glass appearance, and a sibling with CF** = meconium ileus.

stem: A 7-month-old girl has failed to gain weight despite a ravenous appetite. Since the first weeks of life she has had 4 to 5 bulky, greasy, foul-smelling stools daily, and she has had two episodes of pneumonia. Her parents say her skin tastes salty. She has not yet started cereals, and her blood counts are normal.
oneliner: 7-mo F + poor weight gain despite ravenous appetite + bulky greasy foul stools since early weeks + 2 pneumonias + salty skin + no cereals yet, normal CBC → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Begins **after gluten is introduced**; she has not started cereals
whyNot.B: Causes **watery acidic stools without fat malabsorption or poor growth**, and no lung disease
whyNot.C: Pancreatic insufficiency with **neutropenia and skeletal anomalies**; her counts are normal and she has recurrent pneumonia and salty skin
whyNot.E: Gives **bloody stool and eczema**, not greasy stools with pneumonia

why: **Greasy bulky stools with failure to thrive**, **recurrent pneumonia**, and **salty skin** = cystic fibrosis with pancreatic insufficiency.

stem: A 2-year-old girl has had chronic diarrhea with pale, bulky, foul-smelling stools, a distended abdomen, and poor growth since wheat cereal was introduced 4 months ago. She has no lung disease and stool studies for parasites are negative. IgA anti-tissue transglutaminase is high, and her symptoms improve when cereals are removed.
oneliner: 2F + chronic bulky pale foul stools + distended abdomen + poor growth since wheat cereal started + no lung disease, parasites negative + high tTG-IgA + better off cereals → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Presents from early infancy with **lung disease and salty sweat**, not after cereals; she improves off cereals
whyNot.B: Follows **dairy, not wheat**, with no fatty stools, poor growth, or tTG antibodies
whyNot.D: **Trophozoites in stool**; her stool studies are negative
whyNot.E: Affects **middle-aged men with arthritis and PAS-positive macrophages**, with no antibody elevation

why: **Fatty stools and poor growth after wheat**, **positive anti-tTG**, and **improvement off gluten** = celiac disease.

stem: A 22-year-old man has bloating, gas, and watery diarrhea within an hour of drinking milk, but no weight loss or hives, and all symptoms resolve after 2 weeks without dairy.
oneliner: 22M + bloating, gas, watery diarrhea within 1 h of milk + no weight loss or hives + resolves off dairy x 2 wk → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Brings **weight loss and steatorrhea** triggered by wheat, barley, and rye, not only milk
whyNot.B: Causes **hives, wheeze, or anaphylaxis**; he has none
whyNot.C: Persists **regardless of diet** and follows contaminated water
whyNot.D: Pain that **improves with defecation** without a specific dairy trigger

why: **Gas, bloating, and watery diarrhea soon after dairy that resolve when dairy is removed** = lactase (brush-border enzyme) deficiency.

stem: A 6-day-old boy has watery diarrhea with every feed since birth, and his stools are acidic and test positive for reducing sugar. A glucose drink worsens the diarrhea, but a fructose-based formula is tolerated well and he grows normally on it. His mother's cousin had a similar illness.
oneliner: 6-day-old M + watery acidic diarrhea with every feed + stool reducing sugar positive + worse with glucose, fine with fructose formula + maternal cousin affected → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Glucose and galactose are **absorbed normally**; he reacts to glucose
whyNot.C: Reacts to **sucrose and starch**, while glucose is tolerated
whyNot.D: Reacts to **fructose**, which he tolerates
whyNot.E: Gives **blood in stool and eczema**, and is not triggered by a glucose drink

why: **Diarrhea with glucose and galactose but tolerance of fructose**, with a family history = defective SGLT1 transport.

stem: A 52-year-old man has had greasy diarrhea and a 10-kg weight loss, with migratory joint pains for several years and recent double vision. Small-bowel biopsy shows lamina propria filled with foamy macrophages that contain granules staining with periodic acid-Schiff.
oneliner: 52M + greasy diarrhea + 10 kg weight loss + migratory arthralgias for years + recent diplopia + small bowel biopsy: foamy PAS-positive macrophages → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Biopsy shows **villous atrophy with intraepithelial lymphocytes**, without joint or neurologic disease
whyNot.B: Biopsy shows **noncaseating granulomas and transmural inflammation**, not PAS-positive macrophages
whyNot.D: Shows **dilated lacteals with hypoalbuminemia and edema**, without arthritis or diplopia
whyNot.E: Deposits stain with **Congo red (apple-green birefringence)**, not PAS in macrophages

why: **Malabsorption, migratory arthritis, and neurologic signs** with **PAS-positive foamy macrophages** in the small bowel = Whipple disease.

stem: A 45-year-old man has greasy, foul, floating stools and weight loss since a jejunoileal bypass for obesity; a 72-hour collection shows 24 g of fecal fat per day (normal <7 g), and he has no abdominal pain, alcohol use, travel, or gluten-related symptoms.
oneliner: 45M + greasy floating stools + weight loss since jejunoileal bypass + fecal fat 24 g/day (nl <7) + no pain/alcohol/travel/gluten link → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Malabsorption from loss of absorptive surface (bypass)

whyNot.B: Symptoms are tied to **gluten exposure**, not to a surgical bypass
whyNot.C: Needs **alcohol use or recurrent abdominal pain**; he has neither
whyNot.D: Follows **contaminated water or travel** and shows trophozoites in stool
whyNot.E: Gives **watery diarrhea after dairy**, not excess fecal fat

why: **Steatorrhea with weight loss after a jejunoileal bypass** (reduced absorptive surface) = malabsorption syndrome.

stem: A 39-year-old man has lost 15 kg over a year and passes large, pale, floating stools. He now has a scaly, crusted red rash around the mouth and anus and on the hands, with thinning hair and slowly healing wounds. He has no night blindness, bleeding gums, or numbness.
oneliner: 39M + 15 kg weight loss + large floating stools + scaly crusted rash around mouth/anus/hands + hair thinning + slow wound healing + no night blindness/bleeding gums/numbness → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Causes **night blindness, Bitot spots, and dry skin**; none described
whyNot.B: Causes **macrocytic anemia and numbness or ataxia**; no neurologic symptoms
whyNot.C: Causes **bleeding gums and perifollicular hemorrhages**; none here
whyNot.D: Rash is on **sun-exposed skin** (neck, forearms), not around the mouth and anus

why: **Fat malabsorption** with a **periorificial scaly rash, hair loss, and poor wound healing** = zinc deficiency.

stem: A 55-year-old man with chronic pancreatitis has greasy stools and has had bleeding gums and easy bruising for 2 weeks. Hemoglobin is 13.8 g/dL with MCV 90 fL, platelets are 240,000/µL, and prothrombin time is 24 seconds (normal 11 to 13.5).
oneliner: 55M + chronic pancreatitis, greasy stools + bleeding gums, easy bruising + Hb 13.8, MCV 90, platelets 240k, PT 24 s (nl 11-13.5) → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Needs a **low platelet count**; his is 240,000/µL
whyNot.C: Causes **macrocytic anemia** with a normal PT; his MCV is 90 fL
whyNot.D: Causes **neuropathy or high-output heart failure**, not a prolonged PT
whyNot.E: Causes **macrocytosis and neurologic findings** with normal coagulation

why: **Fat malabsorption with bruising, bleeding gums, and a prolonged PT** with normal platelets = vitamin K deficiency.

stem: A 3-year-old boy with cystic fibrosis has frequent bulky, foul-smelling stools and poor weight gain. For a week he has had new bruises on his legs and a nosebleed. Platelets are 310,000/µL, prothrombin time is 26 seconds (normal 11 to 14), and his gums are normal.
oneliner: 3M + known CF + bulky foul stools, poor weight gain + new bruises, nosebleed + platelets 310k, PT 26 s (nl 11-14) + normal gums → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Brings **swollen bleeding gums and perifollicular hemorrhages** with a normal PT; his gums are normal and PT is prolonged
whyNot.B: Normal PT with a **prolonged aPTT or abnormal platelet function**
whyNot.C: Needs a **low platelet count**; his is 310,000/µL
whyNot.E: Causes **anemia and neurologic findings**, not an isolated prolonged PT

why: **Cystic fibrosis fat malabsorption** with **bruising and a prolonged PT** and normal platelets = vitamin K deficiency.

stem: A 73-year-old woman with an irregularly irregular pulse and a diastolic murmur with an opening snap has sudden severe abdominal pain. Her abdomen is only mildly tender and soft. Blood pressure is equal in both arms, serum lipase is normal, lactate is high, and an abdominal x-ray shows distended bowel loops.
oneliner: 73F + irregularly irregular pulse, diastolic murmur + opening snap + sudden severe abdominal pain, mildly tender soft abdomen + equal arm BPs, normal lipase, high lactate → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Gives **colicky pain, obstipation, and prior surgery**; the exam is soft with high lactate
whyNot.C: **Elevated lipase** and pain radiating to the back; lipase is normal
whyNot.D: Pain **migrates to the right lower quadrant with focal tenderness**, not diffuse severe pain with a soft abdomen
whyNot.E: **Tearing pain with unequal arm pressures**; hers are equal

why: **Pain out of proportion to a soft abdomen**, **atrial fibrillation with mitral stenosis** (embolic source), and **high lactate** = acute mesenteric ischemia.

stem: A 64-year-old man who smokes has coronary artery disease and claudication. For 6 months he has had crampy upper abdominal pain 30 to 60 minutes after meals, and he now fears eating and has lost 11 kg. Upper endoscopy is normal, CT shows a normal pancreas, and an epigastric bruit is heard.
oneliner: 64M + smoker with CAD, claudication + crampy pain 30-60 min after meals x 6 mo + food fear + 11 kg weight loss + normal endoscopy and pancreas on CT + epigastric bruit → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Ulcer on endoscopy**; his is normal
whyNot.B: Needs a **pancreatic mass or jaundice**; CT shows a normal pancreas
whyNot.C: Causes **nausea, early satiety, and vomiting of old food**, not pain 30-60 minutes after meals with a bruit
whyNot.D: Needs **alcohol use or pancreatic calcifications**; the pancreas is normal

why: **Postprandial pain, food fear, weight loss, an epigastric bruit, and widespread atherosclerosis** with a normal work-up = chronic mesenteric ischemia.

stem: A 55-year-old man has episodes of facial flushing, watery diarrhea, and palpitations, and a 24-hour urine collection shows high 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid.
oneliner: 55M + episodic facial flushing + watery diarrhea + palpitations + high urinary 5-HIAA → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Causes **episodic hypertension, headache, and high urinary metanephrines**, not high 5-HIAA
whyNot.B: Flushing comes from mast cells, with **high tryptase and urinary histamine**, not high 5-HIAA
whyNot.D: Gives **profuse watery diarrhea with hypokalemia** and no flushing
whyNot.E: Causes **refractory peptic ulcers**, with high gastrin and not 5-HIAA

why: **Flushing and diarrhea with high urinary 5-HIAA** (serotonin breakdown product) = carcinoid syndrome.

stem: A 60-year-old man has episodes of flushing with low blood pressure, crampy diarrhea, and a new systolic murmur at the left lower sternal border that increases with inspiration. CT shows a small mass in the ileal mesentery and multiple liver lesions. His thyroid exam is normal.
oneliner: 60M + flushing with hypotension + crampy diarrhea + new systolic murmur L lower sternal border (louder on inspiration) + ileal mesenteric mass, liver lesions + normal thyroid → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: Causes **hypertensive spells with headache**, not hypotension with a valve lesion
whyNot.C: Gives flushing and diarrhea with a **thyroid mass and high calcitonin**; his thyroid is normal
whyNot.D: Gives **watery diarrhea with hypokalemia** and no flushing or heart murmur
whyNot.E: Gives **urticaria pigmentosa and high tryptase**, and does not damage the right heart valves

why: **Flushing, diarrhea, and a tricuspid murmur** with **liver metastases** (serotonin escapes hepatic metabolism) = carcinoid syndrome.

stem: A 58-year-old man has had cramping midabdominal pain with vomiting for 2 days. He has never had abdominal surgery. A mass is felt in the mid abdomen, and CT shows a bowel-within-bowel target lesion with a polypoid mass at its leading edge.
oneliner: 58M + 2 d cramping midabdominal pain + vomiting + no prior surgery + palpable mass + CT: bowel-within-bowel target with polypoid lead point → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Needs **prior surgery**, and CT shows dilated loops without a telescoped segment
whyNot.B: Shows a **dilated coiled loop with a whirl sign** in an older adult with constipation
whyNot.C: Pain **localizes to the right lower quadrant** and CT shows an inflamed appendix
whyNot.E: **Left lower quadrant pain and fever** with colonic wall thickening and pericolic fat stranding

answer: Intussusception (adult, with a pathologic lead point)
why: **Cramping pain, vomiting, a mass, and a bowel-within-bowel target sign on CT** = intussusception.

stem: An 18-month-old boy has had 2 days of frequent watery diarrhea and vomiting, a sick sibling at home, and now has sunken eyes, dry mucous membranes, and few tears; there is no blood in his stool.
oneliner: 18-mo M + 2 d frequent watery diarrhea, vomiting + sick sibling + sunken eyes, dry mucosa, few tears + no blood in stool → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Episodic colicky pain with currant-jelly stool**; he has bloodless watery stool
whyNot.B: **Chronic** diarrhea and poor growth after gluten, not 2 days of illness with a sick contact
whyNot.C: Causes **bloating after dairy** without vomiting or dehydration
whyNot.E: **Focal right lower quadrant pain with fever**, not watery diarrhea shared with a sibling

why: **Acute watery diarrhea and vomiting with a sick contact and signs of dehydration** = acute gastroenteritis (managed by oral rehydration).

stem: A 68-year-old woman was admitted for pneumonia and treated with ciprofloxacin. On hospital day 6 she develops profuse watery diarrhea with abdominal cramps and a temperature of 38.4 C. White blood cell count is 17,000/µL. She has no recent travel, no sick contacts, and her stools are non-bloody.
oneliner: 68F + hospitalized, on ciprofloxacin for pneumonia + day 6: profuse watery diarrhea, cramps, 38.4 C + WBC 17,000 + no travel/sick contacts, non-bloody → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: Follows **food, travel, or sick contacts**; she has none and onset is days into antibiotics
whyNot.C: Causes **greasy, fatty stools without fever or leukocytosis**
whyNot.D: **Chronic, often bloody** diarrhea with prior flares; hers is acute, non-bloody
whyNot.E: Follows **contaminated water or travel** with subacute greasy diarrhea

why: **Hospital-onset watery diarrhea with fever and leukocytosis days into a fluoroquinolone** = Clostridioides difficile colitis.

stem: A 34-year-old man with HIV infection (CD4 count 60/µL) has had 10 days of watery diarrhea, and stool microscopy with acid-fast staining shows small round acid-fast oocysts.
oneliner: 34M + HIV (CD4 60/µL) + 10 d watery diarrhea + stool acid-fast stain: small round acid-fast oocysts → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Causes **fever, wasting, and acid-fast bacilli** in blood or marrow, not oocysts in stool
whyNot.B: Shows **pear-shaped trophozoites that are not acid-fast**
whyNot.D: Causes **bloody mucoid diarrhea with gram-negative rods**
whyNot.E: Needs **recent antibiotics and toxin in stool**, with no oocysts

why: **Prolonged watery diarrhea in advanced HIV** with **acid-fast oocysts in stool** = cryptosporidiosis.

stem: A 29-year-old woman returned 2 weeks ago from a hiking trip abroad, where she drank untreated stream water. Since then she has had foul-smelling, greasy diarrhea with a lot of gas and a 4-kg weight loss. She has no blood in her stool and no fever.
oneliner: 29F + returned from hiking abroad, drank untreated stream water + 2 wk foul greasy diarrhea, flatulence + 4 kg loss + no blood/fever → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Causes **bloody diarrhea** and liver abscess, with flask-shaped ulcers
whyNot.B: Gives **watery, not greasy** diarrhea that is severe mainly in **immunocompromised** hosts
whyNot.C: Linked to **gluten**, not a sudden onset after drinking untreated water
whyNot.D: **Acute watery diarrhea lasting a few days**, not weeks of greasy stools with weight loss

why: **Untreated stream water** followed by **foul, greasy diarrhea with gas and weight loss**, no blood or fever = giardiasis (trophozoites coat the small-bowel mucosa).

stem: A 21-year-old man develops abdominal cramps and watery diarrhea 24 hours after eating undercooked eggs at a picnic. His temperature is 38.1 C. A stool culture grows a gram-negative rod that does not ferment lactose and produces hydrogen sulfide. His symptoms are already improving with oral fluids.
oneliner: 21M + cramps, watery diarrhea 24 h after undercooked eggs + 38.1 C + stool culture: lactose-nonfermenting, H2S-producing gram-negative rod + improving on oral fluids → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Shigella is **H2S-negative** and causes bloody mucoid stool
whyNot.C: Onset is **1-6 hours** from preformed toxin, with vomiting and no fever
whyNot.D: Grows as **curved oxidase-positive rods at 42 C**, not an H2S-producing rod
whyNot.E: Causes **bloody diarrhea without fever**, and sorbitol-nonfermenting colonies, not H2S production

why: **Egg exposure, fever, and an H2S-producing, lactose-nonfermenting gram-negative rod** = nontyphoidal Salmonella gastroenteritis.

stem: A 27-year-old woman develops sudden vomiting and watery diarrhea 36 hours after a church picnic, and 14 other attendees report the same illness. Her stool contains no blood or white cells. Her husband becomes ill two days later, and everyone recovers within 3 days.
oneliner: 27F + vomiting and watery diarrhea 36 h after a picnic + 14 others ill + no blood or WBC in stool + husband sick 2 d later → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Onset within hours** (preformed toxin) and no person-to-person spread; here onset was 36 h with household spread.
whyNot.B: **Young unvaccinated children** are affected; this is an adult outbreak.
whyNot.D: **Incubation 1-2 weeks** with chronic, greasy, foul stools; this resolved in 3 days.
whyNot.E: **Bloody stool with fecal leukocytes**; here stool has no blood or white cells.

why: **Common-source outbreak, 1-2 day incubation, nonbloody diarrhea without fecal leukocytes, and household spread** = norovirus.

stem: A 3-year-old boy attending day care has had 2 days of cramping and small-volume bloody, mucoid stools with straining after each one. Two classmates are similarly ill. Stool microscopy shows numerous neutrophils.
oneliner: 3M + day-care outbreak + bloody mucoid stools with tenesmus + fecal neutrophils → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **Antibiotic exposure** precedes it; this child has had none and has a day-care outbreak.
whyNot.C: Usually from **poultry/eggs/reptiles**; person-to-person day-care spread with tenesmus points elsewhere.
whyNot.D: **Watery diarrhea without blood** after meat dishes; no day-care spread.
whyNot.E: **Watery, noninflammatory** diarrhea; here stool has neutrophils and blood.

why: **Bloody mucoid stool with tenesmus, day-care spread and fecal neutrophils** = Shigella.

stem: A 31-year-old man develops severe vomiting 3 hours after eating custard-filled pastries that sat at room temperature at a wedding. He has no fever and recovers within a day.
oneliner: 31M + vomiting 3 h after custard pastries left out + afebrile + better in 1 d → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Incubation 6-48 h** with fever and diarrhea; onset here was 3 h with vomiting predominant.
whyNot.B: Emetic form follows **reheated rice**, not cream pastries.
whyNot.C: **Poultry/unpasteurized milk**, incubation 2-5 days, fever and bloody diarrhea.
whyNot.D: **Raw seafood** with watery diarrhea 12-48 h later; no seafood here.

why: **Vomiting within hours of custard left at room temperature** = preformed heat-stable staphylococcal enterotoxin.

stem: A 45-year-old man has watery diarrhea, abdominal cramps and vomiting 24 hours after eating raw oysters at a coastal restaurant. Others at his table are also ill. He improves in 3 days.
oneliner: 45M + watery diarrhea, cramps, vomiting 24 h after raw oysters + others ill → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Onset in **1-6 h** after custard/ham/salads; here 24 h after raw oysters.
whyNot.C: Follows **reheated meat or gravy**, onset 8-16 h.
whyNot.D: Linked to **fried rice**, not shellfish.
whyNot.E: **Poultry**, incubation 2-5 days, often bloody stool.

why: **Raw oysters, 12-48 h onset, watery diarrhea with cramps** = Vibrio parahaemolyticus.

stem: A 16-year-old boy has had 2 days of abdominal pain that began around the umbilicus and moved to the right lower abdomen, with fever of 38.9 C and a WBC of 17,000/mm3. He lies still, and there is guarding and rebound tenderness over the right lower quadrant. CT shows a periappendiceal fluid collection.
oneliner: 16M + 2 d pain migrating to RLQ + fever + WBC 17,000 + guarding/rebound + periappendiceal fluid collection → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Follows a **viral/Yersinia illness** with enlarged nodes and no peritoneal signs; here there is guarding and a fluid collection.
whyNot.B: **Chronic diarrhea, weight loss** over months; this is a 2-day course.
whyNot.C: Classically **painless rectal bleeding** in young children; the **periappendiceal collection** places the problem at the appendix.
whyNot.E: **Left lower quadrant** pain in older adults; here pain is right-sided in a teenager.

why: **Periumbilical pain migrating to RLQ with fever, rebound and periappendiceal collection** = perforating appendicitis.

stem: A 24-year-old man has 4 days of abdominal pain that started near the umbilicus and settled in the right lower quadrant, then fever and diffuse tenderness. At surgery, a ruptured inflamed organ is found with a foul-smelling abscess. Aerobic culture grows only enterococci, yet the Gram stain shows mixed organisms.
oneliner: 24M + 4 d pain periumbilical then RLQ + fever + foul-smelling abscess at surgery + mixed Gram stain, aerobic culture only enterococci → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Typically **older patients with LLQ pain**; this is a young man with right-sided pain.
whyNot.B: **Chronic diarrhea with weight loss**, skip lesions; this is a 4-day course.
whyNot.D: Occurs with **ascites in cirrhosis**, single organism; here a localized foul abscess with mixed flora.
whyNot.E: Usually **painless bleeding** in a child; this migrating RLQ pain with foul abscess is appendiceal.

answer: Ruptured acute appendicitis with periappendiceal abscess
why: **Migrating pain to RLQ, perforation and foul abscess with mixed Gram stain** = ruptured appendix with anaerobes unrecovered.

stem: A 78-year-old woman has had several episodes of painless bright red blood per rectum over 2 months. She has a harsh crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur at the right upper sternal border. stem: A 24-year-old woman has had crampy lower abdominal pain for 8 months that eases after she passes loose stool. Weight, hemoglobin, CRP and stool studies are normal.

stem: A 58-year-old man has a positive fecal occult blood test on routine screening. He has no symptoms. Colonoscopy finds a single pedunculated polyp in the transverse colon, which is removed. A photomicrograph of the polypectomy specimen is shown.

stem: A 4-year-old boy has had several episodes of painless bright red blood on his stools over 2 months. He is otherwise well, and the abdominal and anal exams are normal. Hemoglobin is 10.4 g/dL. Colonoscopy shows a single smooth, round, pedunculated rectal polyp.

stem: A 13-year-old girl has recurrent colicky abdominal pain, and a small-bowel intussusception was reduced last year. She has dark brown macules on her lips and buccal mucosa, and her father has the same macules. Endoscopy shows multiple polyps in the small bowel and colon.

stem: A 21-year-old man has colonoscopy because his father and an uncle both had colon cancer before age 40. Over 200 polyps carpet his colon and rectum. Examination is otherwise normal, with no bony lumps or soft-tissue masses.

stem: A 66-year-old man had a right hemicolectomy and chemotherapy 2 years ago for stage III cecal adenocarcinoma. He now has weight loss, and CT shows several liver masses and multiple small bilateral lung nodules.

stem: A 70-year-old man has fatigue and weakness for 3 months. He reports no change in bowel habits, no pain, and no weight loss. Laboratory results: hemoglobin 9.5 g/dL, MCV 70 fL, ferritin 8 ng/mL, and stool occult blood positive. Endoscopy of the upper GI tract is normal.

stem: A 52-year-old man has had mild fatigue and ALT elevation for 12 years after injection drug use in his twenties. Liver biopsy shows portal lymphoid aggregates, mild macrovesicular steatosis and early periportal fibrosis. HBsAg and ANA are negative, and he does not drink alcohol.

stem: A 60-year-old man died of complications of chronic liver disease after years of alcohol use. A section of his liver stained for collagen is shown.

whyNot.A: **Centrilobular sinusoid dilation** with preserved architecture.

stem: A 49-year-old man who drinks six beers daily has rectal bleeding and mild lower abdominal discomfort. He has scleral icterus, a fluid wave, and visible dilated rectal veins on anoscopy above the dentate line. There is no pain on defecation.
oneliner: 49M + six beers daily + rectal bleeding + ascites + scleral icterus + dilated rectal veins → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Are not caused by the **portal hypertension and liver failure** seen here, and would not explain ascites and icterus.
whyNot.B: **Painless large-volume bleed in an older patient**, no ascites.
whyNot.D: **Weight loss, change in bowel habit**; does not cause ascites and icterus.
whyNot.E: **Hepatic vein thrombosis** in hypercoagulable states, not alcohol use.

why: **Daily alcohol, ascites, icterus and rectal varices** = cirrhosis with portal hypertension (superior to middle/inferior rectal veins).

stem: A 57-year-old man with alcohol dependence has spider angiomata and a hard, nodular liver. Abdominal CT shows a shrunken nodular liver with splenomegaly, and endoscopy shows esophageal varices. Pressure measurement shows raised portal pressure, while the hepatic veins are patent.
oneliner: 57M + alcohol dependence + spider angiomata + shrunken nodular liver + splenomegaly + varices + patent hepatic veins → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: Would show a **focal enhancing mass** and raised AFP.
whyNot.C: **Hepatic veins are patent** here.
whyNot.D: **Prehepatic block with a normal-sized smooth liver**; here the liver is shrunken and nodular.
whyNot.E: A **smooth, enlarged** liver without portal hypertension.

why: **Alcohol, spider angiomata, shrunken nodular liver, splenomegaly and varices** = cirrhosis with portal hypertension.

stem: A 55-year-old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis vomits a large amount of bright red blood. He has jaundice, ascites and caput medusae, and he is hypotensive. He has had no retching before the bleed or epigastric pain.
oneliner: 55M + alcoholic cirrhosis + caput medusae + ascites + large-volume hematemesis + no retching or epigastric pain → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Forceful vomiting with chest pain** and subcutaneous emphysema.
whyNot.B: Follows **retching**, with limited bleeding; none described.
whyNot.C: Prior **aortic graft or aneurysm**.
whyNot.D: **Epigastric pain** with NSAID/H. pylori; no pain here.

why: **Cirrhosis with portal hypertension stigmata and painless massive hematemesis** = ruptured esophageal varices.

stem: A 62-year-old man with chronic hepatitis B and cirrhosis suddenly vomits a large amount of blood and goes into shock. He dies despite resuscitation. A section of the lower esophagus from the autopsy is shown.
oneliner: 62M + HBV cirrhosis + sudden massive hematemesis + shock + [autopsy histology of lower esophagus] → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: A **mass or ulcerated lesion** with dysphagia and weight loss.
whyNot.C: **White plaques** in immunocompromised patients, usually odynophagia.
whyNot.D: **Linear ulcers with intranuclear inclusions** in HIV.
whyNot.E: A **mucosal laceration at the GE junction** after retching.

why: **Cirrhosis with massive hematemesis and dilated submucosal esophageal veins** = ruptured varices from left gastric to azygos shunting.
